solution:
For a wire stretched by a load \(F\), \(Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta L}\), so the elongation is \(\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}\).

The load \(F\) is the same for both wires and they stretch by the same amount \(\Delta L\). Hence \(\dfrac{L}{AY}\) must be the same for both:

\(\dfrac{L_{s}}{A_{s}Y_{s}} = \dfrac{L_{c}}{A_{c}Y_{c}}\)

so that

\(\dfrac{Y_{s}}{Y_{c}} = \dfrac{L_{s}A_{c}}{L_{c}A_{s}} = \dfrac{(4.7)(4.0\times10^{-5})}{(3.5)(3.0\times10^{-5})} = \dfrac{18.8}{10.5} = 1.79\)

The ratio of the Young's modulus of steel to that of copper is \(1.79 \approx 1.8\) (a pure number, no unit).

(a) The graph is a straight line through the origin over almost its whole length, so Hooke's law holds there and Young's modulus is the slope of that line. Reading a point on the straight portion, a strain of \(0.002\) corresponds to a stress of \(150\times10^{6}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\):

\(Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}} = \dfrac{150\times10^{6}}{0.002} = 7.5\times10^{10}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\)

Any other point of the straight part gives the same slope, e.g. \(\dfrac{300\times10^{6}}{0.004} = 7.5\times10^{10}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\).

(b) The yield point is where the curve ceases to be linear and begins to flatten, just before the maximum of the curve. From the graph this happens at a stress of about \(300\times10^{6}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), at a strain of roughly \(0.004\).

(a) Young's modulus \(Y \approx 7.5\times10^{10}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\)
(b) Approximate yield strength \(\approx 3\times10^{8}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\)

Young's modulus is the slope of the initial straight (elastic) part of a stress-strain graph, \(Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}\). Because the two graphs are drawn to the same scale, the slopes may be compared directly by eye.

The initial straight portion of the graph for \(A\) is much steeper than that for \(B\): \(A\) reaches a given stress over a very small strain, whereas \(B\) needs a considerably larger strain to reach the same stress. A steeper slope means a larger \(Y\).

Material \(A\) has the greater Young's modulus.

The strength of a material is the maximum stress it can withstand before it fractures (its ultimate tensile strength). On a stress-strain graph this is the height of the highest point of the curve — not how far the material stretches, which measures ductility rather than strength.

The two graphs are on the same scale, and the curve for \(A\) rises to a slightly greater peak stress than the curve for \(B\) before it turns over.

Material \(A\) is the stronger material.
_note: Measured on the rendered figure (p-11.png): the peak of A stands about 194 px above its own axis against 191 px for B, i.e. A is higher by only ~1.5%. The verdict for (b) therefore rests on A's peak being drawn above B's, and the margin is comparable with the line width — worth an adjudicator's eye. Part (a) is unambiguous by contrast: the fitted initial slopes are 4.87 (A) against 2.85 (B).

solution:
False.

Young's modulus is \(Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}\), so for a given applied stress a material that stretches MORE has a SMALLER value of \(Y\). Rubber extends by several hundred per cent under a stress that would barely deform steel at all, so for rubber the strain in the denominator is enormous and \(Y\) is correspondingly small — of the order of \(10^{6}\) to \(10^{7}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), against about \(2\times10^{11}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\) for steel, a factor of some \(10^{4}\) to \(10^{5}\).

The everyday impression that rubber is "more elastic" because it stretches easily is the opposite of the technical meaning: the material that deforms less for the same stress is the one with the larger elastic modulus.

The statement is FALSE — the Young's modulus of rubber is very much smaller than that of steel.

Both wires have diameter \(0.25\,\text{cm} = 2.5\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), so the radius is \(1.25\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\) and

\(A = \pi r^{2} = \pi(1.25\times10^{-3})^{2} = 4.91\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{2}\)

From Fig. 8.11 the \(4.0\,\text{kg}\) load hangs at the junction of the two wires and the \(6.0\,\text{kg}\) load at the lower end of the brass wire. The steel wire therefore carries both masses, while the brass wire carries only the lower one:

\(F_{\text{steel}} = (4.0+6.0)(9.8) = 98\,\text{N}\), \(F_{\text{brass}} = (6.0)(9.8) = 58.8\,\text{N}\)

Using \(\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}\) with \(Y_{\text{steel}} = 2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), \(L_{\text{steel}} = 1.5\,\text{m}\) and \(Y_{\text{brass}} = 0.91\times10^{11}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\), \(L_{\text{brass}} = 1.0\,\text{m}\):

\(\Delta L_{\text{steel}} = \dfrac{(98)(1.5)}{(4.91\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{11})} = \dfrac{147}{9.82\times10^{5}} = 1.50\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}\)

\(\Delta L_{\text{brass}} = \dfrac{(58.8)(1.0)}{(4.91\times10^{-6})(0.91\times10^{11})} = \dfrac{58.8}{4.47\times10^{5}} = 1.32\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}\)

Elongation of the steel wire \(= 1.5\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}\) (about \(0.15\,\text{mm}\))
Elongation of the brass wire \(= 1.3\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}\) (about \(0.13\,\text{mm}\))
_note: The two loads (4.0 kg at the steel-brass junction, 6.0 kg at the lower end) are printed only in Fig. 8.11 and appear nowhere in the stem; they were read off the rendered page. The key point they settle is that the steel wire bears 10.0 kg and the brass wire only 6.0 kg.

solution:
The cross-sectional area is

\(A = (15.2\times10^{-3})(19.1\times10^{-3}) = 2.903\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}\)

so the tensile stress is

\(\text{stress} = \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{44500}{2.903\times10^{-4}} = 1.533\times10^{8}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\)

The deformation is stated to be elastic, so Hooke's law applies and the strain follows from Young's modulus of copper, \(Y = 1.2\times10^{11}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\):

\(\text{strain} = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{Y} = \dfrac{1.533\times10^{8}}{1.2\times10^{11}} = 1.28\times10^{-3}\)

Resulting strain \(\approx 1.3\times10^{-3}\) (a pure number, no unit).
_note: The stem supplies no modulus, so the chapter's tabulated Young's modulus for copper, 1.2e11 N/m^2, was used. The answer scales inversely with that choice: with the alternative tabulated value 1.1e11 N/m^2 the strain is 1.4e-3. Worth flagging to the cross-check because a widely circulated figure for this exercise (3.65e-3) corresponds to 42 GPa, which is copper's SHEAR modulus and does not apply to a tensile pull; the pull here is longitudinal, so Young's modulus is the correct constant.

solution:
The radius is \(1.5\,\text{cm} = 1.5\times10^{-2}\,\text{m}\), so the cross-sectional area of the cable is

\(A = \pi r^{2} = \pi(1.5\times10^{-2})^{2} = 7.07\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}\)

Since stress \(= F/A\), the greatest force the cable can carry before the stress limit is reached is

\(F_{\max} = (\text{stress})_{\max}\,A = (10^{8})(7.07\times10^{-4}) = 7.07\times10^{4}\,\text{N}\)

The corresponding mass is \(m = \dfrac{F_{\max}}{g} = \dfrac{7.07\times10^{4}}{9.8} = 7.2\times10^{3}\,\text{kg}\).

Maximum load \(= 7.1\times10^{4}\,\text{N}\), that is a mass of about \(7.2\times10^{3}\,\text{kg}\).

The bar is rigid and is supported symmetrically, so it stays horizontal; since the three wires are of equal length \(L = 2.0\,\text{m}\), each must extend by the same amount \(\Delta L\). The tension is also to be the same in each, namely

\(T = \dfrac{Mg}{3} = \dfrac{(15)(9.8)}{3} = 49\,\text{N}\)

From \(\Delta L = \dfrac{TL}{AY}\), equal \(T\), \(L\) and \(\Delta L\) require the product \(AY\) to be the same for every wire:

\(A_{\text{Cu}}Y_{\text{Cu}} = A_{\text{Fe}}Y_{\text{Fe}}\)

With \(A = \dfrac{\pi d^{2}}{4}\) this gives \(\dfrac{d_{\text{Cu}}^{2}}{d_{\text{Fe}}^{2}} = \dfrac{Y_{\text{Fe}}}{Y_{\text{Cu}}}\), so

\(\dfrac{d_{\text{Cu}}}{d_{\text{Fe}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{Y_{\text{Fe}}}{Y_{\text{Cu}}}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.9\times10^{11}}{1.2\times10^{11}}} = \sqrt{1.58} = 1.26\)

The copper wires must be the thicker ones, because copper has the smaller Young's modulus and needs the larger area to stretch by the same amount under the same tension. The mass of the bar fixes the tension but cancels out of the ratio.

\(d_{\text{copper}} : d_{\text{iron}} \approx 1.26 : 1\)
_note: The stem supplies no moduli; the chapter's tabulated values Y(iron) = 1.9e11 N/m^2 and Y(copper) = 1.2e11 N/m^2 were used. The ratio is sensitive to that choice: with the alternative tabulated copper value 1.1e11 N/m^2 it becomes 1.31 : 1.

solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key reads \(1.539 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}\), which is what you get by reading the stem's "2 rev/s" as \(2\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\). That slip reproduces the printed value to four significant figures, which is what identifies it rather than merely disagreeing with it. At \(2\) revolutions per second \(\omega = 4\pi\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\), so the tension at the lowest point is \(mg + m\omega^{2}r \approx 2432\,\text{N}\) and the elongation is \(1.87 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), as derived below.] The cross-sectional area is \(A = 0.065\,\text{cm}^{2} = 0.065\times10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2} = 6.5\times10^{-6}\,\text{m}^{2}\), and the radius of the circle is the length of the wire, \(r = 1.0\,\text{m}\). The angular velocity is

\(\omega = 2\,\text{rev s}^{-1} = 2(2\pi) = 4\pi = 12.57\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\)

At the lowest point of the vertical circle the tension acts upwards and the weight downwards, and their resultant provides the centripetal force:

\(T - mg = m\omega^{2}r\)

\(T = m(g + \omega^{2}r) = 14.5\left(9.8 + (12.57)^{2}(1.0)\right) = 14.5(9.8 + 157.9) = 2.43\times10^{3}\,\text{N}\)

The elongation then follows from \(Y = \dfrac{TL}{A\,\Delta L}\) with \(Y_{\text{steel}} = 2.0\times10^{11}\,\text{N m}^{-2}\):

\(\Delta L = \dfrac{TL}{AY} = \dfrac{(2432)(1.0)}{(6.5\times10^{-6})(2.0\times10^{11})} = \dfrac{2432}{1.3\times10^{6}} = 1.87\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\)

(Using the stretched length \(1.0019\,\text{m}\) as the radius changes this by about \(0.2\%\), which is negligible.)

Elongation of the wire at the lowest point \(\approx 1.9\times10^{-3}\,\text{m}\), that is about \(1.9\,\text{mm}\).
